Leo stopped. He stared at the water bottle in his hand. He unscrewed the cap slowly.

“Crows use twigs as tools,” Leo said. He took a sip, watching Elias over the rim of the bottle. “They bend them to extract larvae from bark. It requires precision.”

Elias blinked. “Okay. So, the adjustment screw? Left or right?”

Leo ignored the question. He walked to the window and looked out at the bare branches of the oak tree in the yard. “*Corvus brachyrhynchos*, the American crow, caches food,” he said. “They remember thousands of hiding spots. They watch you watch them.”

“I need to know about the toilet,” Elias said, his voice rising slightly. “Is it the left-hand thread?”

Leo turned back. He placed the bottle on the counter. “When they recognize a face,” Leo continued, “they hold grudges for years. If you wear a mask once, they scream when you walk by later. Even after five years.”

Elias rubbed his eyes. He could feel the headache forming behind his brow. “Leo. Please. One sentence. Which way does the screw go?”

Leo picked up another box. He began taping it shut, the sound loud in the quiet room. “They mimic car alarms,” Leo said. “Perfectly. Pitch and duration. It’s not random. It’s strategic communication.”

Elias let out a sharp breath. He looked at the pliers in his hand, then at Leo’s impassive face. He realized there would be no help here. Not now. Maybe not ever.

“Righty-tighty,” Elias muttered to himself. He turned and walked back to his apartment.

Leo finished the tape. He smoothed the edge with his thumb. Outside, a single black bird landed on the fence, looking directly into the window.
